items.note: Answers the question directly ('Probably yes, but the data can't prove it'). The before/after evidence checks out: Pro churn was 1 in 23 account-months (Apr–Jun) and 10 in 31 (Aug–Sep), against Basic as the comparison (1 in 24, then 2 in 34). It also explains why the price column can't be trusted.
Removes the 15 trial rows and reports 40 accounts left (20 Basic, 20 Pro), which matches the data.
Removes the 5 @ourco.test rows and notes that keeping them would have added 5 Pro cancellations in August.
Counts an account as churned when cancel_month is filled in. The counts are right: 11 Pro cancellations (1 in May, 7 in August, 3 in September) and 4 Basic.

The summary is mostly in plain language, but it uses terms like 'account-months' and adds a technical caveats section ('active-at-start rule', billing conventions). That level of detail is more than a CEO brief needs.
The Summary section itself has exactly 5 bullets. But the full output adds a 6-bullet Data-quality caveats section and a long chart spec, so the total goes well beyond a summary of at most 5 bullets.

Suggests one chart: monthly churn for Pro vs Basic, with a marker at the July price change. The plotted values are correct. One flaw: the ASCII sketch shows the May Pro point (1/8) at April, though the series list has it right.
Gives a confidence level: moderate that churn rose after the increase, low that price alone caused it. It ties this to the small sample, the unclear price column and the missing cancellation reasons.
